p4-1.text: The question tests fundamental measurement techniques. In part (a), candidates describe an experimental method to measure the time period of a simple pendulum accurately using a stop-watch, which requires timing multiple complete oscillations and calculating the average period. In part (b), candidates match appropriate measurement instruments from a given list to three physical quantities: finding the volume of water in a glass, the width of a small swimming pool, and the thickness of a piece of aluminium foil.

p4-2.text: The question assesses knowledge of vectors, scalars, and motion graphs. In part (a), candidates state the difference between scalar and vector quantities and identify the two scalar quantities from a given list. In part (b), candidates sketch a distance–time graph representing a boat moving at constant speed. In part (c), candidates construct a scale vector diagram to find the magnitude and direction of the resultant velocity of a boat moving due west across a river flowing due south.

p4-3.text: The question concerns linear acceleration and forces acting on a train. In part (a), candidates state the definition of acceleration. In part (b), given the train's mass of 520 000 kg and an acceleration of 1.1 m/s^2, candidates calculate the time taken to increase speed from 15 m/s to 28 m/s, determine the resultant force required to achieve this acceleration using F = ma, and explain why the driving force produced by the motors must be greater than this calculated force due to opposing resistive forces such as friction and air resistance.

p4-4.text: The question examines rocket motion, speed–time graphs, and terminal velocity. In part (a), candidates calculate the initial weight of a rocket from its mass and define the term weight. In part (b), a speed–time graph of the rocket launch is analyzed: candidates describe the motion from O to A and from A to B, and draw a tangent at time t = 400 s to calculate the gradient and determine the acceleration. In part (c), candidates explain in terms of forces (weight and air resistance) why the rocket reaches terminal velocity upon returning through the atmosphere.

p4-5.text: A boat crosses a river at 3.5 m/s perpendicular to the bank, while the river current flows at 2.5 m/s at right angles to the boat's heading. In (a), students must draw a scale diagram or calculate to find the boat's resultant speed and direction relative to the bank. In (b), students state one other scalar quantity and one other vector quantity.

p4-6.text: A swimmer swims across a river at 0.72 m/s perpendicular to a river current of 0.54 m/s. In (a)(i), students determine the magnitude and direction of the swimmer's resultant velocity relative to the bank. In (a)(ii), they calculate the distance travelled in 1.5 minutes. In (b), students explain why the swimmer moves at a constant speed despite exerting a constant forward force.

p4-7.text: A speed–time graph is given for a ball rolling down a ramp and then moving across smooth and rough horizontal surfaces. In part (a), students state the time when the ball reaches the start of the rough section. In part (b), students explain how the graph indicates zero resultant force on the smooth section (constant speed). In part (c), students calculate the acceleration down the ramp using the gradient of the initial straight line. In part (d), students calculate the area under the curve for the first segment to show that the length of the ramp is 9.6 m.

p4-8.text: A non-linear speed–time graph is given for the first 30 s of a space rocket's flight. In part (a), students describe how the acceleration changes between 10 s and 30 s based on the increasing gradient of the curve. In part (b), students draw a tangent at t = 25 s to calculate the instantaneous acceleration. In part (c), students estimate or calculate the distance travelled during the first 10 s by determining the area under the graph.

p4-9.text: A rocket accelerates uniformly from rest to 120 m/s in 8.0 s. Part (a) asks to calculate the acceleration of the rocket. Part (b)(i) asks to plot this initial section of motion on a speed–time graph. Part (b)(ii) requires using the area under the graph to determine the height reached at 8.0 s. Part (b)(iii) asks to complete the speed–time graph from 8.0 s to 25.0 s based on descriptions of decreasing acceleration and subsequent constant speed.

p4-10.text: A speed–time graph shows a person's journey combining walking, waiting, and travelling by bus over 74 minutes. In (a)(i), students calculate the total distance travelled by finding the area under the graph, converting time units appropriately. In (a)(ii), they calculate the average speed for the whole journey. In (b), they state and explain that the gradient of a speed–time graph represents acceleration. In (c), they state and explain the acceleration at t = 40 minutes, where the graph shows constant speed.

p4-11.text: Part (a) asks for a definition of acceleration. Part (b) shows two speed-time graphs (A and B) and two distance-time graphs (C and D), and requires students to describe the motion shown in each of the four graphs, identifying features such as constant speed, deceleration, and increasing acceleration.

p4-12.text: Part (a) defines acceleration. Part (b) provides a distance-time graph for a cyclist's journey. Students must describe the motion during three specific time intervals: 0 to 15 s, 15 to 30 s, and 30 to 40 s. Additionally, students are asked to calculate the average speed and the maximum speed for the 40-second journey using the graph.

p4-13.text: A speed-time graph shows the motion of a bus travelling between bus stops A, B, C and D. Part (a) requires describing the motion between the stops using given terms such as decreasing acceleration or moving forwards at constant speed. Part (b) asks to calculate the distance between A and D using the given average speed of 23 km/h and total time taken. Part (c) involves sketching additional motion on the graph for a stop at D followed by acceleration for 30 seconds, labeling specific points.

p4-14.text: Figure 1.1 displays a distance-time graph for a cyclist travelling between points P and V. Part (a) asks to describe the motion between specific points on the graph (Q and R, R and S, S and T) in terms of acceleration or being stationary. Part (b) requires calculating the speed between U and V using the gradient of the straight-line section. Part (c) asks to sketch a possible continuation of the motion on the graph as the cyclist travels down a steep hill with no resistive forces.

p4-15.text: Part (a) asks to define acceleration. Part (b)(i) requires drawing a speed-time graph for a car accelerating from rest to 28 m/s in 15 s, maintaining constant speed until 32 s, and then decelerating at 2.0 m/s^2 until it stops. Part (b)(ii) considers the car moving in a circle from 15 s to 32 s, asking for the direction of the resultant force and what happens to its velocity.

p4-16.text: Part (a) requires calculating the acceleration at time = 30 s from a given speed-time graph by finding the gradient of the tangent. Part (b) asks to compare the acceleration at 100 s with that at 10 s, and to explain the change in terms of forces. Part (c) requires determining the distance travelled between 120 s and 160 s by calculating the area under the speed-time graph.

p4-17.text: This question tests motion analysis using distance-time and speed-time graphs. In part (a), students draw a constant-speed line on a distance-time graph, state the property representing speed, and calculate average acceleration given initial and final speeds over a time interval. In part (b), students plot a uniform deceleration on a speed-time graph and calculate the total distance travelled over 100 seconds by finding the area under the graph.

p4-18.text: This question examines motion on the Moon using a speed-time graph for a space probe. Part (a) requires determining the acceleration at time = 0 by finding the gradient of the tangent to the curve at the origin. Part (b) asks how the graph shows changing acceleration and why the acceleration changes despite constant motor thrust, linking it to decreasing mass as fuel is consumed. Part (c) involves calculating the distance travelled between 200 s and 300 s by determining the area under the speed-time graph.

p4-19.text: Using a distance-time graph for a moving car, students are asked to: (a) mark a point where acceleration is zero; (b) determine the speed of the car at t = 15 s and the average speed between t = 30 s and t = 45 s; and (c) draw a continuation of the graph showing the car decelerating to a stop by t = 55 s and remaining stationary for 5.0 s.

p4-20.text: Based on a speed-time graph for an ice skater, students: (a) explain deceleration; (b) determine the distance travelled and the average deceleration between t = 3.0 s and t = 6.0 s; and (c) state what happens to the size of the deceleration and the resultant force on the skater after time t = 6.0 s.

p4-21.text: Part (a) asks to identify two vector quantities from a given list. Part (b)(i) requires calculating the final speed of a car accelerating uniformly from rest at 2.2 m/s^2 for 3.0 s. Part (b)(ii) asks for the calculation of the car's average speed given that it travels 9.9 m in the 3.0 s. Part (b)(iii) requires sketching a distance–time graph on the provided axes for the first 3.0 s of the motion.

p4-22.text: Part (a)(i) asks for the definition of the term weight. Part (a)(ii) requires calculating the weight of 350 kg equipment on a planet where the acceleration of free fall is 7.5 m/s^2. Part (b) presents an inflated balloon of mass 80 g and volume 0.30 m^3 released in an atmosphere of density 0.35 kg/m^3, requiring a calculation of the balloon's density to predict and explain its direction of motion.

p4-23.text: This question assesses concepts related to density. In part (a), candidates describe and explain the relative position when oil of a given density is poured onto water of a higher density. In part (b)(i), candidates describe an experimental method to measure the volume of an irregularly shaped solid object using a measuring cylinder. In part (b)(ii), candidates calculate the mass of the object using the density equation given its volume and density.

p4-24.text: This question combines density concepts with motion under terminal velocity. Part (a) asks for the overall density of a stationary weather balloon compared to the surrounding air. Part (b) asks candidates to state and explain whether the balloon rises or falls when the gas inside cools. Part (c)(i) requires sketching a speed–time graph for an object falling from rest through air until it reaches terminal velocity, and part (c)(ii) asks for the initial and final values of acceleration for this motion.

p4-25.text: A block of wood has a volume of 210 cm^3 and a mass of 180 g. Part (a) asks for the calculation of the density of the block of wood. Part (b) states that the block is held above the surface of a liquid with a density of 0.88 g/cm^3 and asks to predict and explain what happens to the block of wood when it is released into the liquid.

p4-26.text: A load is suspended from a thread with a downward vertical force of 0.75 N. Part (a) asks to calculate the mass of the load. Part (b) states a horizontal wire pulls the load with a tension of 1.2 N, requiring the calculation or graphical determination of the magnitude and direction of the resultant force. Part (c) asks to state two changes that forces can produce other than altering an object's size and shape.

p4-27.text: A ball of mass 130 g is launched vertically upwards at 14 m/s until it comes to rest momentarily at height h. Part (a) asks to define deceleration. Part (b) requires showing that the time taken to reach height h is 1.4 s using an acceleration of free fall of 9.8 m/s^2. Part (c) asks to calculate the height h. Part (d) requires describing and explaining the motion of the ball when dropped from the top of a tall building, considering the effect of air resistance.

p4-28.text: A spring suspended next to a metre ruler is loaded with weights, and a reading–weight graph is provided. Part (a) asks to read graph values to find ruler readings for 0 N and 5.6 N load and calculate the extension. Part (b) asks to calculate the spring constant using these values. Part (c) requires calculating the weight of a 0.50 kg object and then determining its acceleration immediately after being pulled down and released when spring tension is 6.5 N.

p4-29.text: This question tests concepts of moments, centre of gravity, and conditions for equilibrium. Part (a) asks for the definition of the moment of a force and the effect it measures. Part (b)(i) asks for the definition of centre of gravity. Part (b)(ii) involves calculating the moment of a 1.3 × 10^7 N block's weight about a base corner using its base dimension of 3.4 m. Part (c) requires stating the two conditions necessary for an object to be in equilibrium.

p4-30.text: This question assesses understanding of Hooke's law and spring behavior. Part (a) requires describing an experimental procedure to determine a spring's spring constant, specifying apparatus, measurements, and calculation steps. Part (b)(i) asks for the definition of the limit of proportionality. Part (b)(ii) requires calculating the extensions of two springs with different spring constants under a 120 N load. Part (b)(iii) asks students to select and justify which spring is more suitable for a baby bouncer using given dimensions.

p4-31.text: A car park barrier arm of weight 60 N is pivoted with a soft iron bar attached at distance d. In part (a), the clockwise moment of the wooden arm about the pivot is calculated, and the distance d needed for equilibrium is determined using the mass of the soft iron bar. In part (b), an electromagnet is placed beneath the soft iron bar. Students describe and explain the movement of the barrier arm when the switch is closed, the effect of decreasing the potential difference across the coil, and why a steel bar would be less effective than a soft iron bar.

p4-32.text: A motorcyclist of combined mass 240 kg accelerates at 7.2 m/s^2 along a straight track from rest for 5.3 s. In part (a), the final speed and the resultant force acting on the motorcycle are calculated. In part (b), the track bends into a circular curve travelled at constant speed. Students state the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity, describe how the velocity changes along the bend, and explain why a resultant force must act on the motorcyclist during circular motion.

p4-33.text: A helium balloon has a mass of 120 kg. In part (a), candidates calculate the weight of the balloon. In part (b), given a resultant force of 54 N, they show that the acceleration of the balloon is 0.45 m/s^2 using F = ma. In part (c), candidates calculate the velocity of the balloon after accelerating from rest for 8.0 s. In part (d), they calculate the distance travelled by the balloon during this 8.0 s interval.

p4-34.text: This question covers spring elasticity and circular motion. In part (a)(i), candidates calculate the spring constant using a given extension–load graph. In part (a)(ii), they mark and label the limit of proportionality, point L, on the graph. In part (b)(i), candidates draw an arrow indicating the direction of the resultant force on a car taking a curved corner. In part (b)(ii), they state how the magnitude of the resultant force changes when the car travels around a corner with a smaller radius.

p4-35.text: A car driver sees an obstruction and applies the brakes after a short delay. Part (a) asks for the definition of deceleration. Part (b) asks for a reason why the car does not decelerate immediately at t = 0. Part (c) presents a distance–time graph, asking for the property of the graph that corresponds to speed and for a calculation of the initial speed v. Part (d) states that a constant braking force F acts, and asks for explanations of why the deceleration is greater than F/m and why the deceleration is not constant.

p4-36.text: A 2.0 kg object on a horizontal bench is connected via a cord over a pulley to a 3.0 kg hanging object, accelerating at 4.0 m/s^2 upon release. Part (a) requires calculating the resultant force on the 2.0 kg object. Part (b) asks for the upward tension force F exerted by the cord on the 3.0 kg object. Part (c)(i) asks to show that the speed after 0.80 s is 3.2 m/s, and part (c)(ii) requires calculating the time taken for a 2.0 cm wide card fixed to the object to pass through a light beam.

p4-37.text: A boat is suspended from a ceiling by two ropes, each with a tension of 75 N at an angle of 60° to the ceiling. In part (a)(i), students draw a vector diagram to determine the magnitude and direction of the resultant force exerted by the ropes on the boat, stating the scale used. In (a)(ii), they use this resultant force to determine the mass of the boat. In part (b), students identify two vector quantities from a given list of physical quantities.

p4-38.text: Part (a) asks students to state two features of a vector quantity and name two examples of vector quantities. Part (b) presents an experiment measuring the length of a spring under different weights, plotted on a length–weight graph. Students determine the initial length of the spring from the graph, explain what is meant by the limit of proportionality and identify the corresponding weight on the graph, and calculate the spring constant of the spring.

p4-39.text: A 62 kg rock climber holds herself in horizontal equilibrium against a vertical cliff using a rope angled at 60° to the horizontal. Part (a) asks to calculate her total weight. Part (b) asks to state the two conditions necessary for an object to be in equilibrium. Part (c)(i) requires calculating the moment of her weight about her feet, given her centre of mass is 0.90 m from the cliff. Part (c)(ii) requires using moments about her feet to determine the tension in the rope, where the rope line intersects her horizontal centre of mass line 1.2 m from the cliff.

p4-40.text: An aeroplane accelerates along a runway for 35 s reaching a final speed of 72 m/s, shown on a non-linear speed–time graph. Part (a) asks to define acceleration. Part (b)(i) requires calculating the average acceleration over the 35 s. Part (b)(ii) requires calculating the average resultant force given a combined mass of 1.1 × 10^5 kg. Part (b)(iii) asks for a reason why acceleration decreases over time despite a constant engine force. Part (b)(iv) requires sketching a graph on given axes showing how the acceleration varies with time.

p4-41.text: The question covers moments, scalar and vector quantities, and vector addition. In part (a), candidates state the definition of the moment of a force about a point and calculate the moment produced about a pivot on a crane arm by a 14000 kg block suspended 20 m away. In part (b), candidates state the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity and give an additional example of each. In part (c), candidates construct a scale diagram to determine the resultant force (magnitude and direction relative to a 20 N force) of two coplanar forces of 20 N and 30 N separated by an angle of 60°.

p4-42.text: The question concerns terminal velocity and forces acting on a 76 kg skydiver who opens a parachute at t = 0. A speed-time graph is provided showing motion from t = 0 to 6.0 s. In part (a), candidates determine the deceleration immediately after the parachute opens from the initial gradient of the graph, and calculate the upward air resistance force acting at this moment. In part (b), candidates explain the skydiver's changing motion between t = 0 and 6.0 s in terms of resultant forces, weight, and drag until a new terminal velocity is reached. In part (c), candidates explain why opening the parachute cannot reduce the speed to zero.

p4-43.text: This question assesses knowledge of moments and equilibrium. Part (a) asks for the definition of the moment of a force. Part (b) presents a diagram of a pivoted L-shaped object in equilibrium and requires calculating an unknown force F using the principle of moments. Part (c) asks the student to describe an experiment using vertical forces to show that an object in equilibrium experiences no resultant moment.

p4-44.text: This question covers scalars, vectors, and vector addition. Part (a) asks how a vector quantity differs from a scalar quantity. Part (b) asks to identify the vector quantities from a provided list. Part (c)(i) requires calculating the weight of a 0.55 kg microphone. Part (c)(ii) asks for a graphical vector diagram to determine the magnitude and direction of the resultant of the weight and a horizontal tension force. Part (c)(iii) asks to compare this resultant with the tension force in the supporting cord for a system in equilibrium.

p4-45.text: Part (a) requires stating Hooke's law. Part (b) presents an extension–load graph of a spring and requires: (i) marking the region where Hooke's law is obeyed, (ii) calculating the spring constant, and (iii) determining the total length of the spring under a given load of 8.5 N when its initial length is 120 mm. Part (c) asks to calculate the mass of an object given its weight of 4.0 N on a planet with a gravitational acceleration of 8.7 m/s^2.

p4-46.text: A speed–time graph shows the first 100 minutes of a ship's journey. Part (a) asks for the maximum acceleration calculated from the steepest gradient of the graph. Part (b) asks for the total distance travelled between 42 minutes and 100 minutes, determined by finding the area under the graph. Part (c)(i) requires calculating the resultant force using F = ma given an acceleration of 0.0087 m/s^2 and a mass of 2.3 × 10^7 kg. Part (c)(ii) asks for an explanation of why the engine force must be greater than this resultant force.

p4-47.text: This question assesses concepts of stability, centre of gravity, and Newton's second law. Part (a) asks candidates to explain why a double-decker bus on a tilted platform starts to topple. Part (b) asks how having 30 passengers on the top compartment and 2 on the bottom compartment affects stability and why. Part (c)(i) requires calculating the combined mass of the empty bus, driver, and 73 passengers. Part (c)(ii) requires calculating the resultant force needed to accelerate the fully loaded bus uniformly from rest to 14 m/s in 20 seconds.

p4-48.text: This question evaluates understanding of terminal velocity, forces during free fall with air resistance, and speed-time graphs. In part (a), candidates label key points on a speed-time graph of a sky-diver: when the parachute opens and the two regions of terminal velocity. In part (b), candidates describe the sky-diver's motion from leaving the balloon to opening her parachute in terms of the forces acting (weight and air resistance). In part (c), candidates calculate her average speed during the first 4.0 seconds of the fall.

p4-49.text: This question assesses understanding of moments and rotational equilibrium. Part (a) asks for the definition of the moment of a force. Part (b) presents a uniform wooden rod suspended from a pivot and held stationary by a horizontal force F; students calculate the weight of the rod, its moment about the pivot, the equal balancing moment produced by F, and the magnitude of force F. Part (c) requires students to state and explain how increasing the angle between the rod and the vertical affects the horizontal force needed to keep the rod stationary.

p4-50.text: This question investigates the motion of objects using different representations. Part (a) uses ticker tape to identify constant speed and asks students to describe and explain the change in motion when a ramp is tilted steeper. Part (b) asks students to calculate distance travelled from the area under a speed-time graph. Part (c) asks for an explanation of the motion of a metal ball falling through liquid from rest to terminal velocity, using concepts of force and acceleration.

p4-51.text: This question examines scalar and vector quantities, basic speed calculations, and motion in a circular path. Part (a) asks for an example of a scalar quantity other than speed, and a vector quantity other than velocity. Part (b) involves a model car travelling around a circular track at constant speed. Students calculate the time for one complete revolution, draw an arrow representing the centripetal resultant force, explain why increasing speed causes the car to leave the track in terms of forces, and draw an arrow showing the car's direction of motion as it leaves the track.

p4-52.text: This question covers the effects of forces on motion and vector diagrams for equilibrium. Part (a) asks students to state three ways a force can alter the motion of an object travelling in a straight line at constant speed. Part (b) shows a 360 N object supported symmetrically by two ropes angled at 45° to the horizontal. Students must draw a scale vector diagram of the forces to determine the tension T in each rope and state the scale used.

p4-53.text: A diagram shows a road sign extending over a road, supported by a post with a concrete block on the opposite side. Students are asked to: (a) calculate the weight of the sign given its mass; (b)(i) calculate the moment about point P due to the sign's weight; (b)(ii) state the meaning of centre of mass and calculate the required weight of the concrete block to balance the moment; (c) state and explain what happens to the moment about point P as the sign and post rotate after the concrete block is removed.

p4-54.text: A speed-time graph shows a car accelerating from rest over 25 s. Students are asked to: (a)(i) determine the acceleration between t = 0 and t = 5.0 s; (a)(ii) calculate the resultant force acting on the car during this time; (b) describe the motion of the car between t = 10 s and t = 15 s and explain how the graph shows this; (c) suggest and explain why the car moves in this way given that the engine force remains constant.

p4-55.text: Part (a) asks to state the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium. Part (b) features a uniform metre rule in equilibrium on a pivot with a 0.50 N load at one end and an upward force F at the other end. Students must (i) draw and label the weight W and reaction force R on the diagram, (ii) calculate F by taking moments about the pivot, and (iii) calculate the upward force R at the pivot.

p4-56.text: Part (a) requires stating the equation defining the moment of a force in words, explaining what is meant by the moment of a force, and explaining the term vector quantity. Part (b) shows a tower crane with a counterweight and a load, asking students to explain how the counterweight prevents the crane from toppling over using the principle of moments.

p4-57.text: Part (a) completes the statement about the moment of a force. Part (b) considers a horizontal rod of length 2.4 m and weight 160 N, suspended by two vertical ropes X and Y with tensions of 80 N each. Sub-question (i) names the point where the weight acts, (ii) calculates the mass of the rod, and (iii) explains using data why the rod is in equilibrium.

p4-58.text: A train of mass 5.6 x 10^5 kg starts from rest and its motion for the first 120 s is represented on a distance-time graph. Part (a)(i) asks for the average speed and the speed at t = 100 s using the graph. Part (a)(ii) compares the acceleration at t = 100 s with t = 20 s. Part (b)(i) calculates the resultant force given the initial acceleration, and part (b)(ii) states the meaning of deceleration.

p4-59.text: A uniform plank AB of length 2.0 m and weight 210 N is suspended horizontally by two vertical ropes X and Y. Rope X is positioned 0.5 m from end A, and rope Y is at end B. (a) State the moment of force P about B in terms of P. (b) Calculate: (i) the moment of the plank's weight W about B; (ii) the tension force P in rope X; (iii) the tension force Q in rope Y using the principle of moments or equilibrium conditions.

p4-60.text: A distance-time graph for a lorry travelling along a straight horizontal road is given. (a) Using the graph, determine: (i) the speed of the lorry at t = 30 s by finding the gradient; (ii) the average speed between t = 60 s and t = 120 s. (b) Given the resistive force at t = 30 s, determine the acceleration and the forward engine force. (c) Describe the motion of the lorry between t = 60 s and t = 130 s by interpreting the shape of the distance-time curve.
